note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §13.7, Stage 65; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiment 20) on data/benches/conductivity.json: electrolytes' conductivity and a conductometric titration. A solution conducts by its ions, each as many as there are and as fast as it moves (Kohlrausch): a strong electrolyte is all ions, a weak one a few in a hundred, water hardly any. In a titration of a strong acid by a strong base, sodium ions take the place of hydrogen ions, which move five times as fast: the conductivity falls to the end point, then rises with the hydroxide left over.
title: Experiment: conductivity and a conductometric titration

report.label: how many times hydrochloric acid conducts acetic acid
report.why: Both are 0.01 M, but hydrochloric acid is all ions and acetic acid about 4 % (its pKa 4.76): their conductivities stand about 25 to 1, the hydrogen ion carrying most of each.

report.label: the end point
report.why: Where the falling line and the rising one cross: before it each drop of base takes away a hydrogen ion (349.6 S cm2/mol) and leaves a sodium (50.1), after it each adds sodium and hydroxide (198.0). The truth is the base that held the flask's chloride's moles, the acid's.

report.label: the acid's concentration
report.why: c = 0.100 x V(end point) / 25.00 mL. The base's label is 0.100 M: it is 0.0997.

steps.title: Your guess
steps.text: Hydrochloric acid and acetic acid, both 0.01 M: how many times better do you think the first conducts? Type your guess, then click "predict".

steps.title: Their conductivity
steps.text: Right-click each beaker in turn and click "+ uS/cm" under its readings: the hydrochloric acid, the sodium chloride, the acetic acid, the water.
steps.why: A strong electrolyte, a weak one, and none: pure water's own ions make 0.06 uS/cm; this water has taken up the carbon dioxide of the room's air (420 ppm), whose carbonic acid adds most of a microsiemens.

steps.title: 25 mL of the acid
steps.text: Pick up the pipette and click the hydrochloric acid of unknown strength: it draws to its mark. Then pick it up again and click the flask.

steps.title: Until it is empty
steps.text: Wait until the pipette has run out.

steps.title: Water to it
steps.text: Pick up the pipette and click its own place. Pick up the water bottle, right-click the flask, type 175 and click "pour".
steps.why: Twelve millilitres of base into 25 mL of acid would dilute it by half, bending both lines; in 200 mL it dilutes it by a twentieth, and the arms stand straight.

steps.title: Fill the burette
steps.text: Pick up the sodium hydroxide, right-click the burette, type 55 and click "pour". Then pick up the burette and click the flask.

steps.title: Log the conductivity
steps.text: Right-click the flask, click "+ uS/cm", then open the notebook and click "1 s".

steps.title: Log the burette
steps.text: Close the notebook, right-click the burette, click "+ mL", open the notebook again and click "1 s".

steps.title: A slow stream
steps.text: Close the notebook, right-click the burette, drag its tap to about 15 % and click 60x.

steps.title: Well past the end point
steps.text: Watch the conductivity fall, then rise again; wait until the burette reads 22 mL.

steps.title: Shut it
steps.text: Drag the burette's tap shut. Open the notebook: x the burette's reading, y the conductivity. Fit a line to each arm away from the bottom; they cross at the end point.
steps.why: Near the end point the curve rounds off (the water's own ions, and the dilution): the end point is where the straight arms meet, not the lowest reading.
